Precision reads: “of all the ones I said yes to, how many were?”. Recall: “of all the ones that were, how many did I catch?”.

And here is the beautiful part: they are the two directions of the same conditional. Precision is $P(\text{it is a yes} \mid \text{I say yes})$ and recall is $P(\text{I say yes} \mid \text{it is a yes})$. Confusing them is exactly the prosecutor's fallacy you already saw with the medical test, and that is why they must always be given together.
La comprobación no es complicada: <stron: The check is not complicated: computing the same measures separately in each group and seeing whether they are alike. The hard part is not the arithmetic, it is remembering to do it and having the data to be able to do it.

Las siglas ROC son de <em>receiver opera: The letters ROC stand for receiver operating characteristic, and they come from the radar operators of the Second World War: you had to decide whether a dot on the screen was an aircraft or noise, and adjusting that sensitivity was literally moving a threshold. The curve moved into the psychology of perception in the fifties and into medicine in the seventies, where it is still the standard way of comparing diagnostic tests. That the same drawing should serve a radar, an eye doctor and a fraud detector says a good deal about how general the problem is.
